Automatically remove the container on exit

stop vs kill: stop politely asks the program to "please exit," giving it a chance to clean up according to the configured stop signal and timeout (defaults depend on the configuration and version); kill pulls the plug.
Removing a container loses the data in its writable layer; named volumes and bind mounts have different lifecycles. Volumes store data on the host and can be shared across containers.
Named volumes vs directory mounts (bind mounts):

Named volumes are managed by Podman. Rootful volumes are usually in /var/lib/containers/storage/volumes/; the rootless location depends on the user’s storage configuration. Use podman volume inspect to look it up; you do not need to know the path in advance
A directory mount specifies a host path directly, making it useful for live code synchronization during development

The installation commands above target mutable distributions; NixOS uses declarations in Nix modules, which an administrator should review and authorize before applying. The database example’s env file must be stored outside the repository with restricted access and supply required values such as POSTGRES_PASSWORD; no valid credentials are provided here. prune, rm, and rmi -f delete resources: inspect dependencies and backups first, as forcibly removing an image may also remove containers that depend on it. A typical port mapping such as -p 8080:80 usually binds to all interfaces; specify loopback explicitly when access should be local only.
